unit.title: Manage personal stress in the workplace

summary: This unit teaches you to understand stress and to manage your own stress at work in a hotel or villa. You will learn what stress is, what causes it in hospitality, how to spot the signs in yourself and others, and how stress can make work unsafe. You will learn healthy ways to cope, how to plan your time, how to speak up calmly, where to get help, and how to make and review a personal stress action plan.

blocks.p: Hotel and villa work is rewarding, but it is also fast, hot, noisy and full of deadlines. Rooms must be ready by check-in. Kitchens must send out orders on time. Guests are sometimes tired, angry or demanding, and you must stay polite. This unit helps you manage the pressure so that you stay healthy, safe and good at your job. It is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees, and it is useful in every job you will ever do.

Stress is not a weakness and it is not a sign that you are a bad worker. Almost everybody feels it. What matters is that you **notice it early, understand what is causing it, and do something sensible about it**. Some of the questions in this unit are about difficult feelings. If a topic upsets you, you may stop and speak to your instructor or the Centre's counsellor.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in a villa or hotel
rows: Say what stress is and how the body reacts
Tell helpful pressure from harmful stress
Name common causes at work, such as workload, long shifts and difficult guests
Name causes outside work, such as money and family worries
Recognise the signs and effects of stress
Spot physical, emotional and behaviour signs in yourself and in others
Explain why stress is a safety risk and how it harms health
Find your triggers and your early warning signs
Use exercise, sleep, food, water, breaks, breathing and support
Know who to turn to at the Centre, at work and in the community
Support a co-worker who is struggling
Make and review a stress action plan
Write a personal plan with causes, goals, steps and support
Check it after a few weeks and change it

flow: Understand stress
Find the causes
Notice the signs
Know your own pattern
Choose healthy coping
Plan your time and speak up
Get help
Make and review a plan

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks. In the practical tasks you make a stress-awareness poster and give a short talk, then take part in role plays and write a personal stress action plan. You may write your plan for a made-up worker if you prefer not to share personal details.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Always follow your workplace's rules and the Centre's student support arrangements. This unit teaches general life skills. It does not replace a doctor or a counsellor.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Stress** is the way your body and mind react when the demands on you feel bigger than your ability to cope. The demand might be a deadline, a noisy kitchen, an angry guest, a bill you cannot pay or an argument at home. The thing that causes the stress is called a **stressor** or a **trigger**.

When you sense danger or a big demand, your brain sets off an automatic alarm called the **fight-or-flight response**. Your body releases hormones such as **adrenaline** and **cortisol**. These get you ready to fight the problem or run from it.

flow: Your brain senses a threat or a big demand
Hormones such as adrenaline are released
Your heart beats faster and you breathe faster
Your muscles tighten and your senses sharpen
The danger passes and your body calms down

blocks.p: This response is useful if you must jump out of the way of a car. It is not useful if the 'danger' is a pile of work that lasts all week. If the alarm keeps ringing and never switches off, the body stays tense and wears out.

head: Feature
Helpful pressure
Harmful stress
rows: Short; it ends when the task is done
Long; it goes on day after day
You feel you have no control
A fair deadline to have a villa ready by 3 p.m. that keeps you focused
Too many rooms every day, no breaks and worry about money, all at once
You do good work and feel proud
Mistakes, illness, poor sleep and burnout

blocks.note: Not all pressure is bad. A little pressure helps you perform. The aim of this unit is not to remove all stress, which is impossible, but to keep it at a level you can manage and to recover from it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Doctors often describe three stages when stress continues.

head: Stage
What is happening
rows: The fight-or-flight alarm goes off. You feel tense and alert.
The pressure continues and your body tries to cope. You may seem to manage, but you are using up energy and may feel tired, irritable or get headaches.
The body and mind can no longer cope. This is where illness, burnout and serious mistakes become more likely.

blocks.p: Stress affects both **physical health** (the body) and **mental health** (thoughts and feelings). The two are linked: a tired body makes the mind worry more, and a worried mind makes the body sleep badly.

blocks.note: People react to the same situation differently. A busy Saturday check-in may excite one room attendant and overwhelm another. Neither is wrong. Do not judge yourself or others by how you each react.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Stress usually has more than one cause, and the causes pile up. A worker who is short of sleep, worried about money and facing a heavy workload feels far more stress than someone with only one of these. Causes fall into two groups: those **at work** and those **outside work**. Outside worries come to work with you.

blocks.h: Causes at work in hotels and villas

head: Cause
Examples in hospitality
rows: Many check-out rooms to turn around before the next guests arrive
A full restaurant and a banquet on the same night
Too few staff in the busy tourist season
Changing rosters that make it hard to plan your life
Conflict with co-workers or a supervisor
Bullying, gossip or feeling unfairly treated
No training for a new task
Heat in kitchens and laundries, noise, steam
Heavy lifting and standing all day
Poor equipment that makes jobs slower
Fear of losing hours or work in the slow season
Little say in how you do your job

ul: Money problems: bills, debts, school fees and the cost of travel to work.
Family problems: arguments, caring for children or a sick or elderly relative.
Long journeys on busy roads and waiting for public transport.
Poor housing, safety worries in the community, or the loss of someone close.
Your own health problems.

blocks.note: Many hospitality workers in Jamaica depend on tips and extra hours. When business is slow, the worry about money can be a large source of stress. Naming the worry is the first step to dealing with it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: The busy season, from about mid-December to April for many north-coast properties, is a time when many properties are short of staff and shifts are long. Plan your rest, food and family time before it starts, and speak to your supervisor early if the load becomes too much.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Things you can change and things you cannot

head: You cannot change
You can change
rows: How early you ask for help
What you do on your days off

blocks.p: Spending your energy on the things you **can** control reduces stress. Spending it on the things you cannot control only makes you more tired.
Stress shows itself in three ways: in your body, in your feelings and in your behaviour. Everyone shows it differently, so learn your own signs and watch for changes in others.

head: Type
Common signs
rows: Headaches and tight neck and shoulders
Feeling tired all the time; trouble sleeping
Catching colds often, because long-term stress weakens the immune system
Feeling worried, anxious or on edge
Snapping at guests or co-workers; arguing
Eating much more or much less

blocks.h: Why stress is a safety problem in hospitality

blocks.p: Kitchens and housekeeping areas have many hazards: knives, hot oil, steam, gas, slicers, cleaning chemicals, wet floors, heavy linen bags and broken glass. Working safely needs your full attention. A stressed, tired or hurried worker is more likely to:

ul: skip a safety step, forget gloves or leave a pan handle sticking out;
mix up or mix together cleaning chemicals;
lift something too heavy alone, or lift with a bent back;
react slowly because of fatigue (deep tiredness);
lose their temper and cause a conflict, or give poor service to a guest.

blocks.note: If stress is stopping you from concentrating on a dangerous task, **make the task safe first**. For example, turn off the burner or put the chemical away. Then tell your supervisor honestly that you cannot focus, take a short break and drink water. It is far better to ask for help than to risk a burn, a cut or a fall.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Area
What can happen if high stress goes on for a long time
rows: High blood pressure, heart problems, stomach problems, weakened defences against illness, constant tiredness
Anxiety, depression, poor memory and concentration
More mistakes and accidents, more days off sick, poor guest service, leaving the job
Arguments with family, friends and co-workers; pulling away from people

blocks.p: **Burnout** is the state of being worn out and drained, physically and mentally, after a long period of too much stress. A person with burnout feels exhausted, stops caring about the work, and may feel that nothing they do makes a difference. Burnout does not go away with one good night of sleep: it needs rest, changes to the workload and often support from others.

blocks.note: Anyone who talks about harming themselves, or says they feel hopeless, must be taken seriously at once. Do not leave them alone. Get your instructor, a supervisor or the Centre's counsellor, and if there is immediate danger call the emergency services.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Knowing your own stress and making an action plan

blocks.p: You cannot manage stress well if you do not know where yours comes from. The first job is to learn your own pattern. The second is to turn what you learn into a plan.
A **stress diary** is a short written record, kept for one to two weeks, of when you felt stressed. It shows patterns you might not notice otherwise.

head: Write down
Example
rows: Four check-outs and only two attendants on the roster
Tight shoulders, heart racing, felt like crying
Rushed, skipped my break, snapped at a co-worker
2: I finished late and felt worse

blocks.p: After one or two weeks, read it through. Look for repeated triggers (a certain shift, a certain task, a certain person), the times of day or week that are worst, and the ways of coping that work and the ones that make things worse.

Everyone has early signs that stress is rising: a clenched jaw, a short temper, trouble falling asleep, skipping meals. If you spot these early, you can act before stress builds up. This is much easier than repairing the damage after a crash.

flow: Find the causes (use your diary)
Pick the main ones to work on
Set a SMART goal and steps for each
Add healthy daily habits
Write your early warning signs
List who can support you
Review after two to four weeks and change it

blocks.p: **SMART** goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. 'Be less stressed' is vague. 'Plan my week on Sunday evening and bring lunch from home on four days out of five, for the next month' is SMART.

head: Part of the plan
Example for a trainee
rows: Falling behind in practical work; the cost of travel to the Centre
Ask my instructor for extra help with bed-making this week
Write a weekly budget for fares and lunch every Sunday for four weeks
Walk 30 minutes, three times a week
Go to bed by 10:30 p.m. on school nights
Drink water, and cut down on energy drinks
My instructor, the Centre's counsellor, my aunt, my church friend
Two weeks from today: what worked, what to change

blocks.note: A plan that is never checked does not help. After two to four weeks, ask: Did this step help? Is the cause still there? What will I change? Keep the steps that work and replace those that do not.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: You are the person responsible for managing your own stress, but you do not have to do it alone. Support from other people is part of a good plan.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Healthy coping looks after the body, calms the mind and deals with the cause. Use several methods together every day, not only when you are already overwhelmed.

head: Habit
How it helps
Practical points
rows: Uses up the energy stress builds up, loosens tight muscles and improves mood and sleep
Walking, football, dancing or cycling; health guides suggest at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week
A rested body and mind think more clearly and cope better with pressure
Most adults need at least 7 hours; keep a regular bedtime where you can; a dark, quiet room; shift workers can sleep in a dark room and avoid screens before bed
Keeps energy steady and avoids hunger and irritability
Fruit, vegetables, protein and ground provisions; do not skip meals during a long shift
Dehydration (losing too much water) makes you tired, irritable and less able to cope
Drink water often in the heat of a kitchen or laundry; take breaks somewhere cool
Too much coffee, tea or energy drinks makes anxiety and poor sleep worse
Keep them for the morning, if you use them

blocks.note: Working in a hot, busy kitchen or laundry in Jamaica's heat is tiring in itself. Drinking water and taking short breaks somewhere cool help your health and your stress levels at the same time.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: **Slow, deep breathing**: breathe in through the nose for about 4 counts, then out slowly through the mouth for about 6 counts. Repeat for a few minutes. It tells your body the danger has passed. It works well during a short break.
**Short breaks**: a few minutes away from the task, in the shade, with water, helps you work better and safer after the break.
**Focus on what you can control**: write down your worries, then circle the ones you can act on today.
**Positive self-talk**: replace 'I can't cope' with 'This is a lot, so I will take it one step at a time.'
**Hobbies, music, faith and family time**: spending time on things you enjoy helps you switch off from work.

blocks.p: Talking to someone you trust, such as a friend, a family member, an instructor, a pastor or a counsellor, often eases worry and helps you see a way forward. You do not need to have the answer before you speak.
Some ways of coping feel like relief but make things worse. Watch out for them in yourself and others.

head: Unhealthy way
Why it does not work
rows: Alcohol, drugs or smoking to relax
Hides the problem for a while, harms health, makes sleep and mood worse, and is unsafe at work
Cutting yourself off from friends and family
You lose the support you need and the worry grows
Skipping meals or eating to comfort yourself all the time
Energy and mood swing up and down
Too much caffeine or energy drinks
Taking it out on others (shouting, arguing)
Ignoring the problem and hoping it goes away

blocks.note: Healthy coping deals with the problem or helps your body recover. Unhealthy coping only hides the feeling for a while.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Managing your time, your words and your guests

blocks.p: A lot of work stress comes from feeling that there is too much to do and not enough time, or from conversations that go badly. Planning and clear, calm speaking give you back a feeling of control.

flow: Write a to-do list of everything that must be done
Sort the tasks by urgency and importance
Do the urgent and important ones first
Break big jobs into small steps
Estimate the time and leave a gap for problems
Tell your supervisor early if you cannot fit it all in

head: Task type
Urgent
Not urgent
rows: Do first. Example: the villa for a guest arriving early at noon
Plan a time. Example: restocking your trolley for tomorrow
Do quickly or ask for help. Example: a small request that someone else can do

ul: Keep your trolley or work station stocked, so that you do not waste trips.
Ask for help early. Waiting until you are far behind only adds to the stress.
Take your breaks, even short ones. Skipping them makes you slower and more likely to make mistakes.

blocks.p: Being **assertive** means saying what you need clearly, calmly and with respect. It sits between **passive** (staying silent and giving in) and **aggressive** (shouting and blaming).

head: Style
What it sounds like
rows: 'You never help me! This is your fault!'
'I have six rooms and the guests arrive at two. Can we agree which ones come first?'

blocks.p: Use **'I' statements**: say how a situation affects you, not what is wrong with the other person. 'I get held up when the towels go missing' is better than 'You always take my towels.'

flow: Wait until you are calm
Ask to talk in private, at a good time
Describe the problem and how it affects you, using 'I' statements
Listen to their side without interrupting
Look together for a fair solution
Agree who will do what
Tell your supervisor if it carries on or if there is bullying or threats

blocks.h: Stay calm with a difficult guest

ul: Remember the guest is usually angry about the problem, not about you.
Keep your voice low and calm; take one slow breath before you answer.
Let the guest finish. Listen, say sorry for the trouble and repeat the main problem back.
Say what you can do and by when.
If the guest becomes abusive or threatening, call your supervisor or security. Do not argue.
Afterwards, take a short break, drink water and tell your supervisor or a co-worker what happened, so you do not carry it through the rest of the shift.

blocks.p: Change, such as a new roster, a new manager or new rules, causes worry because it feels out of your control. Ask the supervisor for the **facts** and how the change affects you. Rumours make worry bigger.

**Work-life balance** means having enough time for work, rest, family and interests. Use your days off to rest and see people. A rested worker copes better and works more safely. If your shifts leave you no time to rest, tell your supervisor before you become exhausted.
Asking for help is a sign of good sense, not weakness. Know who can help before you need them.

head: Place
Who or what
rows: The guidance counsellor or student support staff
The support contacts in the handbook or on the notice board
An employee assistance programme (EAP), if the employer has one: free, private counselling
A doctor at a health centre

blocks.note: Find out now what help your Centre and workplace offer. It is usually in the handbook or from student support staff. Keep the contact details somewhere safe, such as a card in your bag.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: When to see a doctor or other health professional

ul: Stress has lasted for weeks and affects your sleep, eating, health or daily life.
You feel low or hopeless most of the time.
You are relying on alcohol or drugs to cope.
You have physical signs such as chest pain, which need a doctor to check.
You have thoughts of harming yourself. This needs help straight away.

blocks.p: The employer or Centre can reduce stress by planning fair workloads and rosters, giving clear instructions and training, listening to staff, dealing with bullying, providing breaks and a safe place to rest, and telling staff where help is available. Workers should tell their supervisor about problems early, so that the employer can act.

flow: Notice changes: withdrawn, snappy, tired, more mistakes
Choose a quiet, private time
Ask gently if they are OK and listen without judging
Do not give a lecture and do not gossip
Encourage them to speak to a supervisor, counsellor or doctor
Offer to go with them if they want
Check on them again in a few days

blocks.note: Keep what a co-worker tells you private, unless they are in danger. If someone talks about harming themselves, tell your supervisor, instructor or the Centre's counsellor at once and stay with the person until help comes.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: If someone is being bullied or harassed

blocks.p: Bullying is repeated, unfair treatment that hurts or frightens a person. It is a cause of serious stress. A victim should keep a note of what happened, when and who saw it, and report it to the instructor, supervisor or HR, as the policy says. A person who sees bullying should not join in or ignore it: support the person and report it.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, many people find it hard to speak about mental health because of what others may think. Treating a worker who asks for help with respect makes it easier for the next person to ask.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can say what stress is and tell helpful pressure from harmful stress.
I can describe the fight-or-flight response and the roles of adrenaline and cortisol.
I can name causes of stress at work in a hotel or villa and outside work.
I can list the physical, emotional, thinking and behaviour signs of stress.
I can explain why stress is a safety risk and what to do if I cannot concentrate on a dangerous task.
I can say what burnout is and name long-term effects of stress.
I can keep a stress diary and find my triggers and early warning signs.
I can write a SMART goal and a personal stress action plan, and review it.
I can use exercise, sleep, food, water, breaks and slow breathing to cope.
I can say why alcohol, drugs and isolation are unhealthy ways to cope.
I can plan my work with a to-do list and sort tasks by urgency and importance.
I can speak assertively and use 'I' statements.
I can deal calmly with a conflict with a co-worker and with a difficult guest.
I can say where to get help at the Centre, at work and in the community, and when to see a doctor.
I can support a co-worker who seems stressed, and know what to do if they talk about harming themselves.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason as well as the point. For example: 'I take a short break and drink water, because tiredness and dehydration make stress worse and cause mistakes.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Stress
The body's and mind's reaction to pressure or demands that feel greater than you can cope with.
Stressor (trigger)
A thing or event that causes stress.
Fight-or-flight
The body's automatic reaction to danger, which prepares it to fight or run.
Adrenaline
A hormone released quickly when you sense danger; it makes the heart beat faster.
Cortisol
A stress hormone that stays in the body longer than adrenaline.
Helpful pressure
Short, manageable pressure that keeps you focused.
Burnout
Feeling worn out and drained after a long period of too much stress.
Fatigue
Deep tiredness that makes it hard to concentrate and work safely.
Dehydration
Losing too much water from the body; it causes tiredness and irritability.
Resilience
The ability to bounce back after difficult times.
Stress diary
A short record of when you felt stressed, why, how you felt and what you did.
Early warning signs
Your own first signs that stress is rising.
SMART goal
A goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
Assertive
Saying what you need clearly, calmly and with respect.
'I' statement
A way of speaking that describes how something affects you, without blaming.
Prioritise
Decide which tasks come first, by urgency and importance.
Work-life balance
Enough time for work, rest, family and interests.
EAP
Employee assistance programme: free, private counselling and advice offered by some employers.
HR
Human resources: the department that looks after staff matters.
Immune system
The body's defences against illness, which long-term stress can weaken.

c1.title: Christmas week at a bar in Negril
c1.text: Kemar, 22, is a trainee bartender at a beach villa bar in Negril. It is the week before Christmas and the villa is full. He has worked six days in a row, often skipping lunch and living on energy drinks. Tonight he has had two hours of sleep for three nights. At the end of a busy shift he is shaking slightly, his head aches, and he cannot remember a guest's order. He snapped at a waitress an hour ago and now feels ashamed.

c2.title: Money worries in a Kingston laundry
c2.text: Sasha-Kay, 30, works in the laundry of a guest house in Kingston. She is a single mother, her rent is due and her youngest child has been sick. She has stopped eating lunch with the other staff and has begun arriving late. Her supervisor, Mr. Francis, notices that she looks tired and has made several mistakes with the linen counts. The laundry is hot and the washing machines run all day.

c3.title: Assessment week at the Centre
c3.text: Rushane is a trainee at the Centre in St. Catherine. In one week he has a theory paper, a practical assessment and a group poster to finish, and he has also missed some classes because the bus fare is too high. He feels panicky each morning, cannot concentrate and keeps telling himself that he will fail. He has told nobody. His instructor has noticed he is quiet and that his work has slipped.

c4.title: After a difficult guest at an Ocho Rios villa
c4.text: Tanisha, a front desk agent at a villa in Ocho Rios, was shouted at for ten minutes by a guest whose airport transfer was late. The guest then asked for the manager and left a bad review. Tanisha stayed polite, but afterwards she is shaking and close to tears, and there are still three guests waiting to check in. Her co-worker Delroy sees that she is upset.

c5.title: A quiet kitchen helper in Mandeville
c5.text: Donovan, 26, works as a kitchen helper at a hotel in Mandeville. For two weeks he has stopped joining the others at lunch, has been late three times and has told a co-worker, Patrice, 'Nothing matters anymore.' Patrice has noticed he looks exhausted and has started drinking more at weekends. She is not sure whether to say anything.

questions.q: Which group of signs shows that Kemar's stress has reached a level that needs action?
o: A very busy shift, a hot bar, a few mild aches and a good night of sleep to follow
Poor sleep, headache, shaking, memory slips and snapping at a co-worker
Some tiredness at the end of a long day that goes away after dinner and a bath
Pride and excitement after a profitable night, with a little stiffness in his legs
questions.why: Kemar shows physical (shaking, headache), thinking (memory), emotional (shame) and behaviour (snapping, poor sleep and diet) signs together, over several days. A single tired evening would not be a worry.

questions.q: Which change is most likely to help Kemar manage his stress this week?
o: Regular meals, water, a day off and a word with his supervisor about the shifts
An extra energy drink before each shift so that he stays awake and alert for every guest
Working through his breaks so that the queue of waiting guests is cleared a lot faster
A few drinks with the other bar staff after work to help him fall asleep more easily
questions.why: Regular food, water, rest and speaking up deal with the causes and help the body recover. Energy drinks, skipped breaks and alcohol hide the tiredness and make sleep and anxiety worse.

questions.q: Kemar's hands shake while he is cutting limes with a sharp knife. What should he do first?
o: Cut more slowly, hold the limes tightly and concentrate harder until his hands settle
Ask a waitress to finish the cutting while he carries on mixing drinks at the bar
Finish the limes as quickly as he can so that the bar is ready for the next rush
Put the knife down safely, tell the supervisor and take a short break
questions.why: Stress and fatigue make cuts more likely. The safe step is to stop the dangerous task, tell the supervisor and rest, not to carry on and hope.

questions.q: Why did Kemar find it hard to remember the guest's order?
o: Younger workers always have weaker memories than older bartenders in a busy bar
A bartender in a busy bar does not really need a good memory for guests' orders
Stress and tiredness make it harder to concentrate and remember
He did not write the order on a pad, and that is the only cause of the memory slip
questions.why: Poor sleep and long-term stress affect concentration and memory. Writing orders down helps, but the underlying problem here is exhaustion and pressure.

questions.q: Which of Sasha-Kay's changes in behaviour are common warning signs of stress?
o: Working quietly, finishing her linen counts early and leaving on time each afternoon
Chatting more with the team, volunteering for extra work and arriving early each day
Skipping lunch with colleagues, coming in late and making mistakes
Asking her supervisor for a copy of the staff handbook and reading it in her break
questions.why: Withdrawing from others, lateness and more mistakes are typical behaviour signs. They are changes from her normal pattern, which is what to look for.

questions.q: What is the best way for Mr. Francis to approach Sasha-Kay?
o: Say nothing for now and wait to see whether she makes a much bigger mistake first
Speak to her privately, say what he has noticed and ask how he can help
Warn her about her lateness in front of the whole team so that others learn from it
Tell the other staff about her personal problems so that they will all be kind to her
questions.why: A private, caring conversation lets her explain and keeps her dignity. Public warnings or gossip add to her stress and break her trust.

questions.q: Sasha-Kay says she is afraid to take a day off because she needs the money. Which advice is most helpful?
o: Tell her supervisor or HR about her worries and ask what support exists
Work double shifts for a month so that all of her debts can be cleared more quickly
Keep her worries to herself, because talking about them would look like a weakness
Stay home for a few days without telling anyone, so that she can rest and recover
questions.why: Rest is part of staying healthy and safe, and employers can often adjust rosters or point to help. Hiding the problem or working non-stop adds to exhaustion; leaving without telling anyone could cost her the job.

questions.q: Which habit will best protect Sasha-Kay's health while she works in the hot laundry?
o: Drinking sweet sodas through the day to keep her energy up while the machines run
Skipping her breaks so that she can finish the linen early and leave sooner
Wearing thick, heavy clothes so that the steam does not touch her skin at all
Drinking water often and taking short breaks in a cooler area
questions.why: Heat and sweating cause dehydration, which adds to tiredness and irritability. Water and breaks in a cooler place help the body cope.

questions.q: Which action should Rushane take first?
o: Stay home for the week so that he can avoid the feeling of panic each morning
Study through the night every night until all of the assessments are over
Keep quiet, because he thinks that nobody else in the class is struggling like him
Talk to his instructor or the Centre's counsellor about how he feels
questions.why: Telling someone he trusts is the first step and the Centre offers support. Avoiding or overworking makes anxiety and tiredness worse, and many trainees feel the same way.

questions.q: Which part of a stress action plan would help Rushane with his heavy week?
o: A promise to himself to do every single task perfectly or not to do it at all
A long list of everything that could possibly go wrong in each of the assessments
A timetable that sorts tasks by urgency and importance, with breaks and sleep
A plan to leave all of the poster work until the last day, when he feels more pressure
questions.why: A timetable breaks the work into steps and gives a sense of control. Aiming for perfection, dwelling on bad outcomes or delaying the work increases stress.

questions.q: Rushane keeps telling himself 'I will fail'. Which thought would help him most?
o: 'If I just ignore the feeling for long enough, it will go away without any effort'
'This is a lot, so I will take it one step at a time and ask for help'
'Everyone else finds this easy, so there must be something wrong with me'
'Nothing here is under my control, so there is no point in making any plan'
questions.why: Positive, realistic self-talk focuses on what he can do. Ignoring the feeling, comparing himself with others and giving up all keep the stress going.

questions.q: Rushane's bus fare problem is a stressor outside the classroom. Which step best deals with that cause?
o: Make a weekly budget and ask the Centre about fare support
Skip the practical sessions on the days when the fare is hardest to find
Borrow money from several friends without telling any of them why he needs it
Say nothing to anyone and hope that the cost of travel gets cheaper next month
questions.why: Naming the cause and asking about support deals with it directly. Missing classes and hiding problems usually make it worse.

questions.q: What should Tanisha do first to calm herself before the next guest?
o: Take a few slow breaths and a sip of water, then ask a colleague to cover briefly
Tell the waiting guests loudly about the rude guest who shouted at her at the desk
Go straight back to work and say nothing, so that nobody sees she is upset at all
Phone the guest who shouted at her and explain why the guest was in the wrong
questions.why: Slow breathing, water and a short pause help the body calm down. Complaining to guests or arguing is unprofessional, and bottling it up carries the stress through the shift.

questions.q: How can Delroy best support Tanisha?
o: Tell her she is too sensitive for front desk work and that she must toughen up soon
Tell the other guests and staff about what happened so that they can sympathise
Ignore it completely, because it was only a guest shouting and it is part of the job
Offer to cover the desk briefly and ask quietly whether she is all right
questions.why: A kind, private word and practical help show support. Judging her, spreading the story or ignoring her would make her feel worse.

questions.q: Why is it useful for Tanisha to tell her supervisor what happened?
o: It proves to everyone that the guest was completely wrong and that she was right
It means that she will never again have to handle a complaint from any guest
The supervisor can support her and deal with the complaint
It shows the manager that she is not suited to front desk work in the long run
questions.why: Reporting gets her support and lets the property respond to the complaint. It is not about blame or avoiding the job.

questions.q: What should Patrice do about Donovan?
o: Wait for a few more weeks to see whether his low mood passes by itself in time
Speak to him privately and kindly, listen, and encourage him to seek help
Joke with him in front of the other workers to cheer him up and lift his mood
Tell him that he should stop being so dramatic and get on with his daily work
questions.why: Donovan shows several warning signs and has said something worrying. A private, caring talk and a push towards help is the right step. Waiting, joking or dismissing him could leave him alone.

questions.q: When Donovan says 'Nothing matters anymore', what does Patrice need to find out as soon as she can?
o: Whether he is likely to ask the supervisor for extra days off in the coming month
Whether he is thinking of harming himself, so that she can get help at once
Whether he is angry with the head chef over something that happened last week
Whether he is going to repay the money that he borrowed from her last month
questions.why: Statements of hopelessness must be taken seriously. If he is thinking of harming himself, she must not leave him alone and must get the supervisor, counsellor or emergency services.

questions.q: Patrice has begun drinking more at weekends since she noticed Donovan's problem. What is the best advice for her?
o: Treat it as a sign of stress, cut down, and talk or exercise instead
Keep going, because a few drinks at the weekend is a good way to forget about work
Stop speaking to Donovan entirely so that his problems cannot affect her mood
Drink only before her shifts, so that she is more relaxed when she serves guests
questions.why: Using alcohol to cope hides the stress, harms health and is unsafe at work. Helpers need support too: talking to someone and exercising are healthy ways to cope.

questions.q: Which of the following is a healthy way to cope with a stressful shift?
o: A few drinks with colleagues as soon as you are off duty, to wind down quickly
Switching off your phone and avoiding everyone you know for several days
Telling yourself that it is nothing and ignoring how you really feel about it
Slow breathing, then talking it through with someone you trust
questions.why: Breathing calms the body and talking eases the worry. Alcohol, isolation and ignoring the feeling only hide the stress.

questions.q: Which is the best example of an assertive statement to a supervisor who has added more rooms to your list?
o: 'Fine, I will do them all,' said quietly while you feel angry and say nothing more
'You are always giving me far too much work and you never help me out!'
'I have six rooms before two o'clock. Which ones should I do first?'
Saying nothing and doing only the first two rooms, then leaving the rest undone
questions.why: Assertive speech is clear, calm and respectful and invites agreement on priorities. Giving in silently, blaming or leaving work unsaid are passive or aggressive styles.
